entries.description:
Rows and columns held in memory — a table of values. The columns come first: each has a name and a type (Columns.AddColumn). Rows are added with Add and are the table's OWN rows: `row.Amount = 10` changes the table, and a row taken out of it by Find, FindRows or an index is the same row, not a copy. A table is walked with Foreach in row order and read by index, `Table[0]`.

A LINQ query answers with a table (`from o in orders select { Item = o.Item, Amount = o.Amount }`), so the result of a query is read exactly like one made by hand. Ordering by several keys, filtering and grouping are the query's to say — `orderby o.Item, o.Amount descending` — not arguments of the table's own methods.

The table's columns. AddColumn declares one, RemoveColumn takes one away; `Table.Columns[i]` is a column's description, with Name, Types, Caption, Width and Indexing.

Indexing = True on a column that Find and FindRows search by makes them answer through an index built on first use and rebuilt when the rows change, instead of reading every row.
entries.example:
Table.Columns.AddColumn("Code", New TypeDescription("String"));
Table.Columns[0].Indexing = True;   // Find / FindRows by Code use an index

entries.signature: Columns.AddColumn(name : string, type : TypeDescription = String, caption : string = name, width : number)
entries.description: Declares a column and answers with its description. The TYPE decides how the column's cells compare, sort and total — and a column added without one is a STRING column: `AddColumn("N")` followed by `Row.N = 5` holds text, and "5" sorts after "100". Pass the type whenever the column is not text: `New TypeDescription("Number")` holds a number as it is, and `New TypeDescription("Number", New QualifierNumber(15, 2))` keeps two digits after the point. A type named without a qualifier limits nothing: a string of any length, a date with its time.
entries.parameters:
name — the column's name, as rows read it (`Row.<name>`).
type — a TypeDescription; left out, the column holds strings.
caption — the header shown in a form; left out, the name.
width — the width in a form.
entries.return_descr: The column's description (Name, Types, Caption, Width, Indexing).

entries.description: Takes a column away, with its values in every row. A name the table does not have is left alone.

A row of a table: one field per column, read and written by the column's name. A row belongs to its table — writing a field writes the table, and the same row reached twice (by index, by Find, from FindRows) is the same row. A value written into a field is kept as the column's type says.
entries.example:
Row = Table.Find("Paper", "Item");
Row.Amount = Row.Amount + 1;   // the table's row is changed

entries.description: Adds a row at the end and answers with it, every field empty for its column's type.
How many rows the table has. The last row is `Table[Table.Count() - 1]`; an index past it raises.
Removes a row — given as the row itself or by its index. The rows after it move up by one.
entries.parameters: row — a row of this table, or its index from 0.

entries.description: Removes every row. The columns stay.
The first row, in row order, whose field in `column` equals `value` — or Undefined when there is none. On a column with Indexing = True it answers through the column's index.
entries.parameters:
value — what the field must equal.
column — the column's name.
entries.example: Row = Table.Find("Paper", "Item");   // Undefined when no row has it

entries.description: Every row whose fields equal the filter's values — `column = value` for each key of the Structure, all of them at once — in row order. The rows are the table's own. An empty filter answers with every row; a key that names no column raises rather than finding nothing. When a column in the filter has Indexing = True, its index picks the candidates.
entries.syntax_block: Rows = Table.FindRows(New Structure("Warehouse, Item", Warehouse, Item));
entries.parameters: filter — a Structure of column = value.

entries.description: The sum of a column, added exactly — 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.3. An empty field adds nothing and an empty table totals 0. A column that is not there raises, and so does a field that holds something other than a number, naming its row: a wrong total that looks right is the worst answer a sum can give. A column added without a type holds text — declare it as a Number.

Puts the rows in the order of ONE column — the rows themselves move, so the table then IS in that order. Rows with equal values keep the order they had. A column that is not there raises and nothing moves.

An order over several columns, each its own way, is a query's to say: `from r in Table orderby r.Priority, r.Level descending select r`.
entries.parameters:
column — the column's name.
ascending — True (the default) for ascending, False for descending.

entries.description: The values of one column, in row order, as an Array — the way to ask for plain values when a table is what came back. A column that is not there gives an empty Array.
